clue.text: Gruesome when a horse swallows a fly

indicators.note: the horse takes the other piece into its middle, as an animal swallowing something

parts.note: a mare is a female horse
a fly was a light one-horse hired carriage, a kind of cab

explanation.surface: A grisly scene in which a horse gulps down an insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fly' looks like the insect, but in Victorian usage a fly was a light horse-drawn carriage for hire, so the horse here swallows a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something grim and dwelling on death, a horrific scene being the typical example.

clue.text: The first Highlander to put on a topper for the road?

indicators.note: in a down clue the Scotsman wears the other piece like a top hat, sitting above it

parts.note: Mac is a typical Scottish surname prefix, so a Highlander
Adam was the first man

explanation.surface: The leading Scot wearing a top hat for his journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The first' looks like it describes the Highlander, but it is ADAM, the first man, under MAC.
explanation.definitionFit: A road surface of compacted broken stone is named after its Scottish inventor, John McAdam.

clue.text: It supports the hands

parts.note: hands here are the cards dealt to each player, laid out on a piece of furniture

explanation.surface: Something holding up a person's hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A folding table for bridge or whist holds the hands of cards during play.

clue.text: Slag for foundation ?

parts.note: a phosphate fertiliser from steelworks takes this adjective before slag, and the adjective also means fundamental

explanation.surface: Using industrial waste to lay a building's base.
explanation.walkthrough: Basic slag is a fertiliser made from steelmaking waste; the same word means fundamental, the foundation of something.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes what is fundamental, and it also names the steelworks fertiliser called basic slag.

clue.text: Loth ploughmen ?

parts.note: to plough is old university slang for failing a candidate, so the people who plough are those testing students, loth to do it

explanation.surface: Farm workers unwilling to work the land.
explanation.walkthrough: In British university slang to 'plough' a candidate is to fail them in an exam; those who do the failing are reluctant ploughmen.
explanation.definitionFit: Markers who set and judge tests are the ones who plough, that is fail, weak candidates.

clue.text: The old 'uns land the big fish?

explanation.surface: Elderly men hauling in a large catch.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaffer is a country word for an old man, and anglers who land big fish with a gaff hook are gaff-users.

clue.text: Lamp spirit

parts.note: in the Aladdin tale a magical being lives in an old oil lamp and appears when it is rubbed

explanation.surface: Paraffin or meths to fuel a lamp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spirit' suggests lamp fuel, but it is the supernatural being of the Arabian Nights.
explanation.definitionFit: The jinn of Aladdin's story is the magical spirit inhabiting his lamp.

clue.text: Rash to get out of it? Rasher in it

definitions.text: Rash to get out of it? Rasher in it

parts.words: Rash to get out of it? Rasher in it
parts.note: the saying 'out of this into the fire' warns against rash escapes, and a bacon rasher is cooked in the same utensil

explanation.surface: A warning about acting hastily, then a breakfast quip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of the frying pan into the fire' means escaping one trouble only to land in a worse one, hence rash; a rasher is a slice of bacon.
explanation.definitionFit: The cooking vessel of the proverb is the one bacon rashers are fried in.

clue.text: Oddly named place of Scotland

indicators.note: done oddly, the word is set out in a strange order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Scottish place with a peculiar name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' rearranges NAMED.
explanation.definitionFit: A village in the Scottish Borders near Kelso, birthplace of the poet James Thomson.

clue.text: An ungenial hesitancy is hard to the breast

definitions.note: the clue's phrase describes the hard part at the breast, standing for the bony noun

parts.note: ungenial means unfriendly, stern
um is the sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: A gruff hesitation hurts someone's feelings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard to the breast' sounds like an emotional blow, but it is the bone at the front of the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: The breastbone is the hard flat bone at the centre of the chest.

clue.text: Is critical of a hook-up ?

explanation.surface: Someone grumbling about a connection being made.
explanation.definitionFit: To complain and find fault is a sense of the verb, while freshwater fish of that name end up on an angler's hook.

clue.text: A canny one to cause trouble

indicators.note: the shrewd figure is made to cause a new arrangement, the letters being put to work in a different order

explanation.surface: A shrewd person stirring up mischief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to cause' tells you to rework A CANNY ONE into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Irritation and bother are what trouble brings, so the noun for vexation fits.

clue.text: He too may look for a clue in print

definitions.text: He too may look for a clue in print

parts.words: He too may look for a clue in print
parts.note: like the crossword solver, a sleuth hunts clues, perhaps a fingerprint, and also figures in printed fiction

explanation.surface: Someone, like the solver, searching for a clue in a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleuth's whole job is seeking clues, including the prints left at a crime scene.

clue.text: A second name for Princess Ida's University ?

explanation.surface: A request for another title for the women's college in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's Princess Ida the princess runs a university for women only, from which males are barred; the answer split in two says just that.
explanation.definitionFit: In Roman naming the gens name came second, after the praenomen; and Ida's college admitted no males.

clue.text: She turns tail to marry Thorpe in Lincs

definitions.text: She turns tail to marry Thorpe in Lincs

parts.words: She turns tail to marry Thorpe in Lincs
parts.note: a girl's name with its last two letters swapped, joined to Thorpe, gives the seaside town Mablethorpe in Lincolnshire

explanation.surface: A woman running away to wed a man called Thorpe in Lincolnshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Mablethorpe is a seaside resort in Lincolnshire, an English county; swap the girl's final two letters and add THORPE to reach it.
explanation.definitionFit: The girl's name is the woman meant by 'She', the start of the Lincolnshire town once her tail turns.

clue.text: State where they drank Bourbon ?

parts.note: bourbon is the American whiskey, but the American state was named after Louis XIV, a king of the House of Bourbon, toasted there

explanation.surface: Asking which American state drinks whiskey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bourbon' looks like the whiskey of Kentucky, but this state was named for Louis XIV of the French royal House of Bourbon.
explanation.definitionFit: The US state named in honour of the French Bourbon king Louis XIV.

clue.text: The making of a spirit of medium body

definitions.text: The making of a spirit of medium body

parts.words: The making of a spirit of medium body
parts.note: seance lore says a medium exudes a substance from the body out of which spirits take shape

explanation.surface: Producing a ghost of average build.
explanation.walkthrough: 'medium' looks like average size, but it is the seance medium whose body gives off the stuff ghosts are made from.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiritualists claimed this viscous emanation from a medium formed visible ghosts.

clue.text: Tall story of six spouses ?

explanation.surface: A far-fetched tale about someone with six husbands or wives.
explanation.walkthrough: An old British term for the third floor, reached by three pairs of stairs, so a high storey; three couples make six spouses.
explanation.definitionFit: A room up three flights of stairs is on a high floor, and three couples contain six spouses.

clue.text: Our countrymen brought to their knees

definitions.text: Our countrymen brought to their knees

parts.words: Our countrymen brought to their knees
parts.note: the English kneeling, members of the Church of England at prayer

explanation.surface: The English humbled in defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought to their knees' suggests defeat, but it means kneeling in church.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the Church of England, an English church, kneel to pray.

clue.text: He's first to get his oath out ?

definitions.text: He's first to get his oath out ?

parts.words: He's first to get his oath out ?
parts.note: split as pre-curser, one who swears before everyone else

explanation.surface: A man who is quickest to swear.
explanation.definitionFit: A forerunner comes first, and read in two parts the word is someone who curses beforehand.

clue.text: Bird the Psalmist placed where no politician wishes to be

definitions.text: Bird the Psalmist placed where no politician wishes to be

parts.words: Bird the Psalmist placed where no politician wishes to be
parts.note: Psalm 102 says 'I am like a ... of the wilderness', and a politician out of office is said to be in the wilderness

explanation.surface: A bird put somewhere a politician dreads.
explanation.walkthrough: Psalm 102:6 has the bird 'of the wilderness'; politicians out of power are 'in the wilderness'.
explanation.definitionFit: The large pouched water bird that the Psalmist sets in the wilderness.

clue.text: La, my foggy love!

annotationWithheld.why: La, my foggy love! (5): NIGEL; no parse found for how the clue gives the name (no anagram or hidden run fits), and no source explains the allusion

clue.text: Woodmen who keep diaries ?

explanation.surface: Foresters who keep journals.
explanation.definitionFit: Lumberjacks fell trees, and people who keep a log or record are recorders of that kind.

clue.text: House of bats ?

parts.note: the House in Parliament shares its name with the London cricket ground that is the home of the bat

explanation.surface: A roost where bats live.
explanation.walkthrough: LORD'S is a London cricket ground, the home of English cricket, while the House of Lords is Parliament's upper chamber; 'bats' are cricket bats, not the flying animals.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper chamber of Parliament and the famous cricket ground in St John's Wood share the name.

clue.text: About to turn Cobbett's London to something modern

definitions.note: the phrase stands with 'turn' for the verb make fresh again

parts.note: re means about, concerning

indicators.note: turning the nickname round means reading its letters from the back

parts.note: William Cobbett called London the Great Wen, a wen being a swelling

explanation.surface: Ready to make the radical writer's London up to date.
explanation.walkthrough: William Cobbett, the 19th-century English radical, called London 'the Great Wen'. 'turn' reverses WEN.
explanation.definitionFit: To restore or make fresh is to turn something back into a new state.

clue.text: Like Milton's ears at a touch of the sun

definitions.text: Like Milton's ears at a touch of the sun

parts.words: Like Milton's ears at a touch of the sun
parts.note: in Lycidas Milton writes that Phoebus 'touch'd my ... ears', Phoebus being the sun god

explanation.surface: The poet's ears reacting to a bit of sunburn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the sun' is Phoebus Apollo, who in Milton's Lycidas touches the poet's quivering ears to rebuke him.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's own adjective for the ears is quivering, shaking at the god's touch.

clue.text: Words a twaddler has to eat

definitions.text: Words a twaddler has to eat

parts.words: Words a twaddler has to eat
parts.note: a talker of nonsense utters rubbish, and the same word is offal eaten as food

explanation.surface: Someone talking nonsense forced to take it back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eat his words' suggests retraction, but the word is both nonsense and cow's stomach served as food.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonsense talk and edible cattle stomach lining share this name.

clue.text: Has a spending spree — what remorse!

explanation.surface: Someone splashes out and then regrets it.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'blue' money is old British slang for squandering it.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang says one squanders money, and a fit of low spirits is the gloom that follows.

clue.text: Italian is her field of work

definitions.text: Italian is her field of work

parts.words: Italian is her field of work
parts.note: an Italian countrywoman who labours in the fields, the Italian word for a peasant woman

explanation.surface: A woman whose professional subject is the Italian language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'field of work' looks like an academic specialism, but it is a literal farm field.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian word for a female peasant, a woman who works the land.

clue.text: To you and me advancing years are habit-forming

definitions.note: the clue uses an adjective, but it stands for the noun meaning established custom

parts.note: you and me together are us
growing older is age

explanation.surface: As we get older our routines set in.
explanation.definitionFit: Customary practice, the way things are habitually done, is the noun's sense.

clue.text: Something novel and swinging for fringe people

parts.note: novel means new
a gate is something that swings on its hinges

explanation.surface: A fresh, lively entertainment for an avant-garde crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'Newgate fringe' was a beard worn under the chin, named after London's Newgate prison, so the name belongs to those wearing such a fringe.
explanation.definitionFit: The old London prison gave its name to the chin-beard called a Newgate fringe, worn by such people.

clue.text: Counters a crazed sorority

indicators.note: something crazed is driven mad, so the word for the sorority is thrown into a new order

parts.note: a sorority is a sisterhood, so its members are sisters

explanation.surface: A deranged group of women fighting back.
explanation.definitionFit: To withstand or oppose something is to counter it, both verbs in the third person.
